content: The objective of the SEARCH study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of prolonged use of more intensive cholesterol-lowering therapy in patients who were at high cardiovascular risk. The study, titled Study of the Effectiveness of Additional Reductions in Cholesterol and Homocysteine (SEARCH), was a randomized, double-blinded clinical trial. It included 12,064 men and women aged 18 to 80 years, all of whom had a history of myocardial infarction. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either homocysteine-lowering therapy with 2 mg of folic acid plus 1 mg of vitamin B12 daily or a matching placebo. The primary endpoint of the study was the occurrence of major vascular events. These events were defined as coronary death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or arterial revascularization. Among the participants, those receiving 80 mg of simvastatin experienced a 0.35 mmol/L greater reduction in LDL cholesterol compared to those receiving 20 mg of simvastatin. This corresponded to a 7% greater reduction in LDL-C levels in the 80 mg group. Overall, the group receiving 80 mg of simvastatin demonstrated a 6% reduction in major vascular events compared to the group receiving 20 mg of simvastatin. However, 0.3% of patients in the 20 mg simvastatin group experienced adverse effects. The conclusion of the SEARCH study was that it failed to demonstrate a significant benefit from more intensive cholesterol-lowering therapy. This was partly due to a substantial number of patients in the 20 mg simvastatin group taking additional statins outside the study protocol, as more aggressive LDL-C targets were introduced during the study period.
